questions.question: What is useReducer and when should you use it instead of useState?
questions.title: Usereducer Basics
questions.direct_answer: useReducer manages state through a pure reducer function: (state, action) => newState. You dispatch actions; the reducer computes the next state. Use it when: multiple sub-values update together (related state), the next state depends on the previous in complex ways, or you want update logic testable and centralized. useState for simple independent values; useReducer for state machines and complex transitions.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D[dispatch action] --> R[reducer: pure fn]
    R -->|returns NEW object| N[next state]
    N --> RR[re-render]
    D -.batched, in order.-> R
    subgraph purity
        P[same state+action → same result]
        NM[no mutation, no side effects]
    end
    T[unit test: table-driven] --> R
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The dispatch batching difference (the mechanism): useState setters batch and apply functional updates in order. useReducer dispatches queue actions the same way — the reducer runs for each queued action against the previous result, so a burst of dispatches composes correctly (dispatch(increment) ×3 → reducer called 3 times, each seeing the last). This is why reducer-based rapid updates don't have the stale-state hazard of setState(count+1) — the reducer always receives the CURRENT state at apply time, like the functional form of setState but structured.

The Redux lineage (the design context): useReducer IS the Redux core API (Dan Abramov built both). Redux adds on top: a global store, middleware for side effects, DevTools time-travel via action log. useReducer is the same update model scoped to one component — and the jump from useReducer + Context to Redux is incremental (state at Context provider, dispatch exposed via context) until you need middleware/persistence/devtools.

The reducer-vs-actions design judgment (the senior close): a good reducer file reads like a spec of the domain — action types enumerate WHAT CAN HAPPEN (ADD_ITEM, REMOVE_ITEM, APPLY_DISCOUNT), the switch cases read as invariants (ADD_ITEM never touches discount state). Action payloads stay minimal data; derived values (totals) compute at render or in selectors, never stored in reducer state. The testability payoff: reducer unit tests are plain table-driven tests — [state, action, expectedState] rows — no rendering, no mocking.
